assignment: Post #2 research ledger -- 'Optimizing for ads inside free LLM answers.' Covers, per-assistant as of 2026-09: (a) ad status (ChatGPT tiers, Google AI Mode/AI Overviews, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, Meta AI), (b) free-vs-paid audience split per assistant, (c) ad targeting/labeling and what advertisers can buy today, (d) measured effects -- CTR, trust studies, regulator/disclosure guidance, (e) the organic-citation side and whether ads and citations interact, (f) concrete quarter-actionable levers for a small business or consultant with cost/eligibility stated.
researcher_note: Retrieved live via WebSearch/WebFetch on 2026-09-24, single session, roughly 60 tool calls (well under the ~150-call time-box). Confidence convention matches content-studio/research/2026-09-14/search-intent/data.json and the 2026-09-22/zero-click-future ledger: high = primary source directly fetched and quoted verbatim; medium-high = primary source identified and consistent across multiple independent outlets, but the primary itself returned HTTP 403 to direct WebFetch (this affected nearly every openai.com and help.openai.com URL attempted this session -- OpenAI's own policy pages were consistently unreachable by this tool this pass, same pattern the 2026-09-22 researcher hit); medium = single directly-fetched secondary/aggregator source reporting a named primary, or a WebSearch synthesis corroborated across 3+ independent outlets; low-medium = WebSearch synthesis only, corroborated by 2 or fewer outlets, or a single vendor/industry blog; low = single source, unverified, paywalled, or explicitly forward-looking/not-yet-in-effect. Several entries in this ledger are deliberately flagged as DISAGREEING or UNRESOLVED rather than resolved to one number -- see notes.md.
does_not_duplicate: content-studio/research/2026-09-22/zero-click-future/data.json already carries, sourced and dated, the four starter entries this post brief named: chatgpt_ads_timeline (section e, the Jan-Aug 2026 rollout milestones), chatgpt_sponsored_agents (section e, the original 2026-09-16 announcement), perplexity_ads_lifecycle (section e, the full 2024-11-12 to 2026-02-18/19 arc with $20K/$34M figures), and google_ai_mode_ads (section e, the Google Marketing Live 2026 format announcement) -- plus alphabet_ad_revenue_share and alphabet_fy2025_revenue_breakdown (section c) for the 'more than 70% of Alphabet revenue is advertising' economic backdrop, and the Pew Research 8%-vs-15% AI-Overview CTR study. None of those eight are re-entered here. Several entries below explicitly say 'expands' or 'cross-reference' where this pass added NEW detail (partner names, mechanics, later-stage figures) on the same underlying topic -- those are additive, not duplicative, and say so in their own note field.

stats.metric: Meta AI — no sponsored placements inside chat answers yet; monetizes via downstream ad targeting instead
stats.source: Proton, DataSlayer, TechCrunch, MediaPost, about.fb.com
stats.publisher: Meta (per own product announcements + secondary reporting)
stats.note: Two distinct mechanisms, worth separating clearly in the post: (1) Since 2025-12-16, Meta uses users' Meta AI conversations to personalize ads shown elsewhere on Facebook/Instagram/WhatsApp/Messenger — affects the reported 1B+ MAU base, no opt-out. This is NOT an in-answer ad, it's conversation-data-to-ad-targeting. (2) Since March 2026, Meta is testing a shopping-recommendation carousel INSIDE Meta AI chat responses (web browser only, limited US users) — product cards with images/prices/links, no checkout in-chat. Meta has not disclosed whether carousel results are influenced by advertiser relationships or commission, and a spokesperson declined to answer whether Facebook/Instagram advertisers get priority placement. No confirmed 'Sponsored' label mechanic equivalent to ChatGPT/Copilot found this pass — flag as the least-transparent of the six ad statuses researched.

stats.metric: Share of ChatGPT commercial prompts that show an ad, and how many are off-target
stats.unit: percent of commercial prompts showing an ad; 14.35 percent judged off-target
stats.source: SE Ranking, 'ChatGPT Shows Ads for 1 in 4 Commercial Prompts'
stats.note: Methodologically transparent, independently reproducible study: 50,006 commercially-oriented prompts across 20 US niches (~2,500/niche). Relevance judged via cosine similarity between prompt/ad/answer embeddings, benchmarked against shuffled random pairs, plus manual review of a flagged sample. Corroborated by Search Engine Land's independent write-up (reports 26%, rounding). Single-study source — not yet replicated by a second independent researcher — hence medium-high not high.

stats.metric: ChatGPT weekly active users vs. paid subscribers, with computed conversion rate
stats.source: digitalinformationworld.com and techcrunch.com reporting on OpenAI's own Feb 2026 disclosure
stats.publisher: OpenAI (per multi-outlet reporting of company disclosure)
stats.note: OpenAI reported 900M weekly active users (up from 800M in October 2025) and 50M+ paid CONSUMER subscribers (across Plus/Pro/Go), separately 9M+ paying business users and 1M business customers. Arithmetic shown, computed this pass from OpenAI's own two disclosed figures: 50,000,000 / 900,000,000 = 5.56% ≈ 5.6% consumer paid-conversion rate. This means roughly 94-95% of ChatGPT's consumer weekly active user base is on an ad-eligible (Free or Go) tier or is a business/enterprise seat outside this ratio — the single most load-bearing number for the post's 'what share of answers can even carry an ad' framing.

stats.metric: Gemini app monthly active users vs. paid subscribers (Google does not disclose the split)
stats.unit: MAU disclosed, paid undisclosed, third-party estimate only
stats.source: blog.google (usage figure, official), implicator.ai / techtimes.com (analysis noting the non-disclosure), getpanto.ai (third-party paid estimate)
stats.note: Gemini app passed 1 billion MAU on 2026-08-11 (Google's own announcement, high confidence on this half). Google has never disclosed a paid-subscriber count for any AI tier. Third-party industry estimate (not Google-sourced, methodology not disclosed by getpanto.ai): 15-25 million paying subscribers 'as of early 2026' against a base the estimate itself states as 'then-750 million MAU' — implying roughly 2-3% conversion AT THAT EARLIER, SMALLER MAU BASE. Arithmetic shown, computed this pass and clearly separated from the source's own claim: applying that same 15-25M estimate to the newer, Google-confirmed 1B MAU figure would imply 1.5-2.5% — this recomputation is mine, not sourced, and drops further because MAU grew while the paid estimate did not update; flag as directional only, not a citable figure on its own.

stats.metric: Perplexity MAU vs. paid share — internally inconsistent figures found
stats.source: resourcera.com (paid-count estimate) alongside sentisight.ai and demandsage.com (conversion-rate estimate), Perplexity itself discloses neither
stats.publisher: Third-party estimates only, Perplexity has not disclosed
stats.date: MAU milestone dated 2026-04; paid estimates undated within 2026
stats.note: Perplexity passed 100M+ MAU in April 2026 (122% growth from 45M at end of 2025) — medium confidence, widely repeated. Paid share is where sources disagree: one estimate puts paid users at ~1 million (~1% of 100M), while a separate estimate in the same search cluster states 'conversion rates from free to Pro hover around 5-7%' — those two figures are arithmetically inconsistent (5-7% of 100M would be 5-7M, not 1M). NEITHER is Perplexity-disclosed. Additional confound: millions of 'Pro' seats were given away free (e.g., a 360-million-eligible-customer Airtel bundle in India), so any paid-count estimate that doesn't separate purchased-vs-gifted Pro seats is likely unreliable. Do not cite a single Perplexity paid-conversion number in the post without this caveat attached.

stats.metric: How ChatGPT targets ads to users — pre- and post-personalization-opt-in signals
stats.source: Help Net Security, quoting OpenAI's privacy policy/help center directly
stats.note: Before a user opts into ad personalization: targeting uses only the CURRENT conversation's topic, general location, and device type. After opting in: targeting adds in-product activity, ads previously interacted with, and broader conversation context. Users get an explicit opt-in choice ('opt in, or don't') and can change it later in settings. Advertisers reportedly receive only aggregate performance data (views, clicks) — not chat content or identity.

stats.metric: ChatGPT Ads Manager — self-serve buying terms: budget floor, verification, countries
stats.source: topgrowthmarketing.com, trylapis.com, and OpenAI Help Center pages (help.openai.com/en/articles/20001213 and /20001245 both returned HTTP 403 to direct WebFetch this session)
stats.note: No waitlist in the queue-priority sense: any eligible business in a supported country can sign up directly at ads.openai.com. $25/day minimum PER CAMPAIGN (no separate account-level minimum) — this replaced a $200,000 minimum spend that applied when ads first launched in February 2026, before self-serve opened. OpenAI enforces spend caps: up to 2x the daily budget on a high-demand day, but total 7-day spend capped at 7x the daily budget. Countries as of 2026-08-24: US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, plus 31 European markets. Business verification required via Persona (identity + sanctions screening) before a campaign can run.

stats.metric: ChatGPT ad exclusion/brand-safety controls for advertisers — limited relative to mature platforms
stats.source: eMarketer ('ChatGPT ad exclusions give brands safeguards as targeting gaps persist') and contentgrip.com
stats.note: OpenAI supports custom-audience inclusion/exclusion, geographic targeting, campaign objectives, and 'contextual guidance' for ad groups — but explicitly, contextual guidance is NOT a keyword match, audience rule, or placement guarantee. OpenAI is separately testing true negative/exclusion targeting (letting advertisers flag contexts they don't want ads to appear near) but only with a small advertiser group as of retrieval — not generally available. Restricted categories: adult content, alcohol, tobacco, gambling outright excluded; health, financial, political, and legal ads face tighter review. Net comparison point for the post: advertisers have materially LESS placement control in ChatGPT than in mature Google/Microsoft search advertising.

stats.source: Google Ads Help (support.google.com), fetched directly

Existing Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns become automatically eligible for AI Overview placement if they win the auction AND address both the query and the AI Overview's content — no separate sign-up or campaign type required. Sensitive verticals excluded: adult, alcohol, gambling, finance, healthcare, politics, 'and more.'

stats.unit: percent of ad impressions judged off-target

stats.metric: Google AI Mode: share of commercial queries with ads, and how rarely the advertiser is also cited
stats.unit: percent of commercial queries showing a text ad; separately, 11 percent domain-citation overlap and 1.95 percent exact-URL overlap
stats.source: SE Ranking, 'AI Mode shows ads on 1 in 3 queries: 50K keywords studied,' corroborated by Search Engine Journal's independent write-up
stats.note: Same publisher/methodology family as the ChatGPT study above (cosine-similarity-style keyword sampling, preselected to trigger text ads, sampled evenly across niches). Directly answers the assignment's question about whether Google's AI Mode ads and citations interact: for keywords that show a text ad, the advertiser's domain appears anywhere in the AI Mode answer's citations only 11% of the time, and the exact advertised URL only 1.95% of the time. Strongest available quantitative evidence (this pass) that paying for an AI Mode ad does not meaningfully buy citation presence. Cost-per-click correlated with ad frequency: 24% ad-presence rate below $2 CPC, rising to 53.6% above $10 CPC. Caveat stated by the source itself: 'reflects results on one date, not ad prevalence across commercial searches' — a single-day snapshot, not a tracked trend.

stats.unit: percent who rate AI-assistant ads at least as trustworthy as Google Search ads
stats.exact_quote: "The consumers in this survey are the people who set the norms that the mainstream inherits." — Nataly Kelly, CMO, Zappi
stats.source: Zappi, fetched directly

stats.source: The Information (Shane Burke)

This figure sits in sharp apparent tension with the Zappi 82%-trust figure above, but the two surveys likely measure different populations and different questions (Zappi = existing AI-assistant users specifically asked to compare AI ads to search ads; The Information = broader/different 'chatbot users' framing, mechanism unclear). stats.metric: First independent academic audit of ChatGPT ad targeting — income-based disparity finding
stats.exact_quote: "Lower-income accounts, regardless of race, are more likely to receive ads."
stats.source: Lurie, Encarnaón, Friedler, Metaxa, "The Beginning of ChatGPT Ads," arXiv preprint, accepted AAAI/ACM AIES 2026
stats.note: The first published empirical/academic (not vendor-funded) study of ChatGPT's in-answer ads. Methodology: 91 'sock puppet' accounts engineered to signal different racial/ethnic identities and income levels, 335 prompts, yielding 3,000+ ad impressions from 186 unique advertisers. KEY FINDING: lower-income-signaling accounts received ads at a higher rate than higher-income accounts, REGARDLESS OF the race/ethnicity signal tested — an equity/fairness finding with no vendor-published counterpart. Secondary findings: ads began appearing 14 days after account creation (not immediately); ad content skewed toward consumer goods and toward driving users to an advertiser generally rather than a specific product; ads were visually separated from ChatGPT's own responses. Strongest single 'measured effect' source in this research pass — independently designed, methodologically disclosed, peer-review-track.

stats.metric: FTC's general AI-in-advertising disclosure framework — applies to AI-generated/AI-mediated ad content broadly, not written for in-answer chatbot ads specifically
stats.source: Multiple law-firm/compliance-blog secondary sources (FTC.gov itself not directly fetched this pass)
stats.publisher: Federal Trade Commission (per secondary legal-compliance reporting)
stats.date: staff guidance 2025-03; AI enforcement unit launched 2026-01; penalty figure current for 2026
stats.note: SCOPE CAVEAT: no FTC action or guidance specifically targeting in-answer/conversational-AI ad placements (ChatGPT, Copilot, or AI Overview ads) was found this pass — this is the FTC's general AI-content and endorsement-disclosure framework being applied by industry commentators, not a chatbot-ads-specific rule. Core requirement being reported: 'dual disclosure' — AI-involvement and commercial-relationship are treated as two SEPARATE required disclosures; a single '#ad' or single 'AI-generated' label does not satisfy both. Dedicated FTC AI enforcement unit reported launched January 2026. Maximum civil penalty for undisclosed synthetic endorsements reported at $53,088 per violation (2026 inflation-adjusted figure per one source) or $51,744 (per a different source in the same search) — the two figures disagree slightly; treat as 'approximately $51-53K per violation' rather than citing either as exact without a primary FTC.gov figure.

stats.metric: California SB 1050 — AI-generated performer disclosure in ads (signed same week as this research, narrower scope than in-answer ads)
stats.source: gov.ca.gov (Governor's press release)
stats.publisher: State of California / Office of the Governor
stats.note: SCOPE CAVEAT for the post: SB 1050 requires disclosure when an AI-GENERATED PERFORMER (synthetic actor/voice) appears in a video or audio ad — this governs AI in ad PRODUCTION/creative, not AI placing or generating ads inside a chatbot's conversational answers. Do not conflate with in-answer ad disclosure; it's a different regulatory target that happens to be dated the same week as this research pass. Signed by Gov. Newsom, authored by Sen. Angelique Ashby, ~3.5 months before taking effect.

stats.metric: EU AI Act Article 50 — AI-system disclosure requirement now in effect; governs 'is this an AI' not 'is this an ad'
stats.source: Travers Smith, Faegre Drinker, artificialintelligenceact.eu legal-compliance summaries
stats.note: SCOPE CAVEAT: Article 50 requires providers of AI systems that interact directly with people to ensure users are informed they're dealing with an AI system, unless obvious from context — applies at first interaction with each new individual, not just once generally. This is AI-disclosure (chatbot vs. human), NOT ad-disclosure (sponsored vs. organic) — relevant backdrop for the post's regulatory section but should not be presented as an ads-specific rule. A statement buried in T&Cs or a bare 'AI-generated' watermark does not satisfy it per the sources. Penalty: up to €15 million or 3% of global annual revenue, whichever is higher.

stats.metric: UK ASA — signaled intent to scrutinize AI-in-ads, no formal chatbot-ad-specific guidance published as of retrieval
stats.source: resultsense.com summary of ASA public statements
stats.publisher: UK Advertising Standards Authority (per secondary reporting)
stats.note: Lowest-confidence regulatory item in this ledger: the ASA's Chief Executive has said publicly that both ads FOR AI products and ads USING AI are 'on the radar,' and that advertisers will be held responsible for AI-produced content — but no formal CAP guidance specific to conversational-AI ad placement had been published as of retrieval. Sources characterize further guidance or enforcement as 'reasonably expected during 2026,' i.e., anticipated, not existing. Do not cite as an active rule.

stats.metric: Cross-LLM citation-source diversity and overlap — how differently four assistants cite the same queries
stats.unit: percent agreement across all four LLMs on citing the identical domain for the same query
stats.source: Bill Widmer / Orbit Media Studios, fetched directly
stats.note: Automated weekly tracker (built with Claude Code per the source), 72 prompts x 3 B2B websites, running for roughly the 3 months through 2026-08-23: 13,184 citations analyzed across 1,765 answers, spanning ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity. Average sources cited per answer varies sharply by platform: Perplexity 19.2/answer (leans heavily on LinkedIn, YouTube, Reddit), Gemini 8.1/answer (Reddit and listicles), ChatGPT 4.5/answer (primary sources and vendor documentation), Claude 3.6/answer (review sites and curated listicles, and per the source 'never cited Reddit' in the sample). HEADLINE FINDING: only 1.7% agreement across all four models on citing the SAME domain for the SAME query — strong evidence that 'getting cited' is a per-platform exercise, not a single generalizable SEO/GEO task. One independent tracker, single-website-cluster (3 B2B sites) — flag as not yet cross-validated by a second research group, hence medium-high not high.

stats.metric: Whether structured data/schema markup causes higher AI-citation rates — actively disputed this quarter, not resolved
stats.unit: disputed causal claim, two studies disagreeing
stats.source: BrightEdge (73-site analysis, cited via secondary aggregation) vs. Ahrefs (1,885-page test) vs. Kurt Fischman, SSRN preprint
stats.publisher: Multiple, disagreeing (none independently re-fetched verbatim this pass)
stats.date: BrightEdge claim and Ahrefs test both circulating in 2026 coverage; SSRN paper dated 2026-02
stats.note: FLAG PROMINENTLY IN THE POST rather than picking a side: one source cluster (attributed to BrightEdge, via secondary aggregation, not independently re-fetched) claims sites with structured data/FAQ blocks see a 44% increase in AI-search citations, and that 73 analyzed sites with proper schema were cited 3.2x more often. A DIRECTLY CONFLICTING claim: Ahrefs reportedly tested 1,885 pages and found NO uplift in AI citations across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, or AI Mode from schema markup alone. A third, more academically-framed source (Kurt Fischman, 'Does Schema Markup Predict AI Citation? A Cross-Platform Empirical Study,' SSRN, 2026-02) leans toward the skeptical side per synthesis. None of the three was independently re-fetched verbatim this pass — all via WebSearch synthesis only. The pattern itself (industry-vendor content claiming a tactic works vs. a larger, more controlled test finding no effect) recurs across this whole research area and should probably be a named caution in the post, not just a footnote.
